title: Very Hot Beverages Linked To Triple Esophageal Cancer Risk, Major Study Finds
excerpt: A study of nearly a million UK adults found those who prefer drinks 'very hot' face more than triple the risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma — but researchers stress it's the heat, not the chai, that matters.
body:
• The largest study to date — nearly 980,000 middle-aged adults in the UK — found people who prefer "very hot" beverages have more than triple the risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
  • Drinking six or more hot drinks a day raised the risk by 71%, even after accounting for how hot people liked them.
  • The danger is heat, not the drink: tea and coffee at warm temperatures carried no such link, and adding milk made no difference if the drink stayed hot.
  • WHO's cancer agency has classified beverages above 65°C (149°F) as "probably carcinogenic to humans" since 2016; researchers advise letting drinks cool a few minutes before sipping.

Your morning chai is not the problem. Its temperature might be. The largest study ever conducted on hot beverages and cancer, covering nearly 980,000 middle-aged adults in the UK, found that people who prefer their drinks "very hot" face more than triple the risk of one type of esophageal cancer.

The research, drawn from the Million Women Study and the UK Biobank, tracked participants for an average of 14.2 and 11.1 years respectively, recording 2,348 cases of esophageal cancer. Just under half of the participants reported drinking six or more hot drinks a day, and about 15% said they preferred them "very hot."

Compared with people who preferred their drinks merely warm, those who liked them hot had nearly double the risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma; those who liked them very hot had more than three times the risk. Quantity compounded the effect: six or more hot drinks a day was associated with a 71% higher risk even after the researchers controlled for temperature preference.

"This is the largest study to date, and it does really add to the evidence that drinking very hot and hot beverages could increase the risk of this type of cancer."

— Keren Papier, senior nutritional epidemiologist, Oxford Population Health

Context & Background

The finding lands on ground the World Health Organization mapped a decade ago. In 2016, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified drinking very hot beverages — consumed above 65°C, or 149°F — as "probably carcinogenic to humans" (Group 2A). The classification rested on studies of maté in South America, and hot tea in China, Iran, Japan, and Turkey, where researchers found esophageal cancer risk climbing with drink temperature.

"These results suggest that drinking very hot beverages is one probable cause of oesophageal cancer and that it is the temperature, rather than the drinks themselves, that appears to be responsible."

— Christopher Wild, director, IARC (2016)

Animal studies supplied the mechanism: liquids at 65°C and above promoted tumor development in rats and mice, suggesting repeated thermal injury to the esophageal lining drives the damage. A case-control study in Malawi and Tanzania found "very hot" versus "hot" food or drink raised risk 1.92-fold, and people with the highest thermal-exposure scores were 4.6 times as likely to develop the cancer.

The UK study extends the evidence to a Western population. One detail carried over: whether participants added milk made no difference to the risk — provided the drink stayed hot.

Impact & Analysis

Tripling a small risk still leaves a small risk. The lifetime risk of this cancer in the UK is about 1%, so even a three-fold increase keeps most individuals' absolute risk low. The proven levers remain the old ones: not smoking and cutting back on alcohol.

But temperature is an independent factor — and a controllable one. In the US, hot beverages are commonly served between 140°F and 160°F (60–71°C), straddling the 149°F threshold. Clinical nutritionist Adriana Salmon of MD Anderson advised simply waiting for drinks to cool or choosing cold versions.

One caveat: the UK cohorts reported preferred temperature rather than measured cups, so the exact danger zone for everyday tea and coffee still needs work.

Diaspora Angle

This one lands close to home. Indian households serve chai boiling, order it "kadak," and treat piping-hot rasam, milk, and soup as comfort by definition. None of that changes the science: the drink is innocent, the scalding is not. Pour the cup, wait a few minutes, skip the first searing sip. Tradition survives; the burn doesn't have to.

What's Next

The mechanism is still being worked out — Cancer Research UK part-funds the PROMINENT team investigating how heat damages the esophageal lining. Until that picture sharpens, the message is simple: let it cool down. Quitting smoking and limiting alcohol remain the highest-impact moves by a wide margin.
